hops.afterHeading: Two questions for any sensory cell
hops.title: Vampire bats retune a pain channel to find warm prey
hops.text: Common vampire bats find warm spots on their prey with infrared-sensing nerve fibres that serve pit organs on the face. Evidence points to TRPV1, which in human sensory neurons responds to painful heat. In the ganglia serving the bat's face, alternative splicing slips a stop codon into the transcript, and roughly two in five TRPV1 transcripts there encode a channel with a shorter tail. Tested alone in lab cells, the short form switched on near 30 degrees C and the full-length form near 40; in body-serving ganglia, over 97 percent of TRPV1 transcripts are full-length. No enzyme sits between heat and pore, so editing the channel retunes the sense.

sources.citation: Gracheva EO et al. Ganglion-specific splicing of TRPV1 underlies infrared sensation in vampire bats. Nature 476:88-91 (2011)
Gracheva EO et al. 2011, full text (PMC3535012): TRPV1-S is 35-46% of trigeminal TRPV1 transcripts, under 3% in dorsal root ganglia; thresholds 30.5 vs 39.6 degrees C

hops.afterHeading: Where a cascade's gain comes from, and what it costs
hops.title: Total darkness does not silence your rods
hops.text: You might assume that in a sealed, pitch-black room your rods go quiet. They do not. Now and then heat alone flips a rhodopsin molecule, and the rod produces an electrical blip that looks just like its response to one real photon. The cascade amplifies the false alarm as faithfully as a real one. Across species, fewer estimated false alarms went with lower light thresholds, though later frog experiments showed shorter signal summation and lower flash sensitivity also mattered. The weakest flash a person reliably detects produces about 10 to 20 rhodopsin isomerizations; one long-standing idea is that this noise is why we cannot reliably see a single photon.

hops.afterHeading: The checklist for calling something the transducer
hops.title: The mustard-oil channel once proposed as the hearing channel
hops.text: In 2004, David Corey's lab, the same Corey as the forty-microsecond study, proposed TRPA1 as a candidate for the hair cell's transduction channel. It passed place and time: its mRNA appeared just as hair cells became mechanosensitive, antibodies labelled the bundles, and blocking its expression reduced hair-cell responses in zebrafish and mice. Then came the loss test. In 2006 two groups, one of them Corey's own, deleted Trpa1 in mice. The mice startled normally to loud noise, kept their balance, and had normal hearing responses and vestibular hair-cell currents. Instead, their pain responses to mustard oil were weakened or lost, depending on the test.
